extraction.name: BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions, paired with Wikipedia passages, designed to test inferential abilities.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified (first word in a manually constructed set of indicator words and sufficient length). Questions were kept only if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results. Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: decide if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; find a passage within the document containing enough information to answer; mark whether the answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions training set were included.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered to those likely to be yes/no by checking if the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and of sufficient length. Only questions with a Wikipedia page in the first five search results were kept. Annotators selected a passage within the document containing enough information to answer. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer were used, paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: first, decide if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; second, for good questions, find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer; third, mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Annotators could mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to yes/no questions and Wikipedia passages. The questions are typically short (average length 8.9 tokens) with longer passages (average length 108 tokens). The dataset may not cover all types of inference needed for general question answering.
